His verses on releasing [an animal?] and healing a crane—the transcription here reads “放DRU療鶴” [?]—include the lines: “Preserving life, not killing, brings hidden merit”; “In distress, seeking the aid of divine beings to save the life remaining.” His verses on leaping fish and the appearance of carp include the lines: “Even in tender years, filial devotion can be steadfast”; “A spring emerging beside the dwelling is truly a wondrous event.” His preface explains that a single good thought communicates with the spirits. Is this not reasoning from Heaven and finding confirmation among human beings?

Great indeed are these imperial words! Resplendent as fine jade, they all bear directly upon the enduring moral norms of the people. They form warp and weft with the teaching concerning the promulgation of words; they do more than extend imperial glory into the future and rival the renown of former sovereigns. Thus, throughout the realm, households transmit them and individuals recite them, reducing their faults and returning to the supreme standard. Pure customs flourish in harmony, and the influence of imperial teaching spreads abroad. All under Heaven has enjoyed profound harmony for nearly a hundred and eighty years and more, down to the present day.

Now our present Emperor, reverent and enlightened, sagely and divine, has answered the mandate of the age by bringing about a restoration, magnifying…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
聖業大新物覩慨然
慕古六詩之義而發爲篇章形于諷誦者尤
未易殫述是故
平臺有咏勵臣鄰也
大報有歌揚洪眷也除夕有作崇脩省也感
雨有吟恤民隱也
天藻奎章紛綸葳蕤蔚乎盛矣又嘗因儒臣進
講大學衍義感賦五言古詩十韻
君倡臣和彙爲一帙總名之曰翊學詩竊嘗伏
===
讀一二曰致治貴有本本端化自平曰正
心誠其意志定必不遷卽蕩蕩平平之義
也曰身脩本心正家國治同然曰國治乃
昭明萬邦斯協焉卽會極歸極之義也曰
於變帝堯典思齊文王篇曰萬化脩身始
朕念方拳拳卽皇建有極之義也旣又
親灑
宸翰以
賜輔臣而一時賡和之詞莫非皇極敷言之
punctuated: 聖業，大新物覩，慨然慕古六詩之義，而發爲篇章、形于諷誦者，尤未易殫述。是故平臺有咏，勵臣鄰也；大報有歌，揚洪眷也；除夕有作，崇脩省也；感雨有吟，恤民隱也。天藻奎章，紛綸葳蕤，蔚乎盛矣！又嘗因儒臣進講《大學衍義》，感賦五言古詩十韻，君倡臣和，彙爲一帙，總名之曰《翊學詩》。竊嘗伏讀一二，曰：「致治貴有本，本端化自平。」曰：「正心誠其意，志定必不遷。」卽蕩蕩平平之義也。曰：「身脩本心正，家國治同然。」曰：「國治乃昭明，萬邦斯協焉。」卽會極歸極之義也。曰：「於變帝堯典，思齊文王篇。」曰：「萬化脩身始，朕念方拳拳。」卽皇建有極之義也。旣又親灑宸翰，以賜輔臣，而一時賡和之詞，莫非皇極敷言之
translation_en:
…the sagely enterprise, bringing about a great renewal manifest to all things. Deeply moved to emulate the meaning of the ancient six forms of poetry, he has expressed it in compositions and given it voice in recitation; these works are especially difficult to recount exhaustively. Thus his verses on the Platform encourage his close ministers; his song for the Great Sacrifice of Requital proclaims Heaven’s abundant favor; his composition on New Year’s Eve honors self-cultivation and reflection; and his poem on being moved by rain expresses concern for the people’s sufferings. His celestial compositions and stellar writings are profuse and luxuriant—how splendidly they flourish!

Once, moved by the Confucian ministers’ exposition of the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning (Daxue yanyi), he composed an ancient-style poem in five-character lines with ten rhymes. The sovereign led and his ministers responded in verse; these were collected in one volume, collectively entitled Poems in Support of Learning (Yixue shi). I have humbly read some of them with reverence. One passage says: “To achieve good government, having a foundation is essential; / When the foundation is upright, transforming influence naturally brings peace.” Another says: “Rectify the mind and make its intentions sincere; / Once the resolve is fixed, it surely will not waver.” These express the meaning of “broad and level” in the Great Plan. Another passage says: “Cultivating the person rests on rectifying the mind; / Ordering the family and state follows the same principle.” Another says: “When the state is ordered, there is radiant clarity; / The myriad states then come into harmony.” These express the meaning of gathering at and returning to the supreme standard. Another passage says: “‘Oh, what a transformation!’ in the Canon of Emperor Yao; / ‘Thinking on his dignity’ in the ode to King Wen.” Another says: “All transforming influence begins with cultivating the person; / My thoughts now dwell earnestly upon this.” These express the meaning of “the sovereign establishes the supreme standard.”

Afterward, he personally inscribed these works in his imperial hand and bestowed them upon his grand secretaries. The poems composed in response at that time all expressed the…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
旨我
皇上所以闡明詩敎囿天下于皇極而遠追三
百篇之轍者無不會其精深詣其純粹故
二紀以來遵道者丕變覲
聖者奕新而
大典微言揭如日星
鴻恩濊澤同乎天地所以上符
二祖遠繼唐虞三代之盛者端見於此而非漢
唐宋諸君之所敢望矣然執事猶拳拳下
===
===
問欲歌咏其一二用宣揚
聖明蕩蕩平平之化愚又何言哉蓋古之忠愛
之臣務賛揚其君之美凡以風天下後世
俾其習於耳浹於心而不忘也故有周盛
時濟濟多士一則曰周王壽考遐不作人
一則曰古之人無斁譽髦斯士所以咏歌
文王之德者凡以歸極也今
皇上躬親師帥以詩敎天下固巳光四表而格
上下矣然豈無其本哉仰惟
punctuated:
旨。我皇上所以闡明詩敎，囿天下于皇極，而遠追三百篇之轍者，無不會其精深，詣其純粹。故二紀以來，遵道者丕變，覲聖者奕新，而大典微言揭如日星，鴻恩濊澤同乎天地。所以上符二祖，遠繼唐虞三代之盛者，端見於此，而非漢唐宋諸君之所敢望矣。然執事猶拳拳下問，欲歌咏其一二，用宣揚聖明蕩蕩平平之化，愚又何言哉？
蓋古之忠愛之臣，務賛揚其君之美，凡以風天下後世，俾其習於耳，浹於心而不忘也。故有周盛時，濟濟多士，一則曰：「周王壽考，遐不作人？」一則曰：「古之人無斁，譽髦斯士。」所以咏歌文王之德者，凡以歸極也。今皇上躬親師帥，以詩敎天下，固巳光四表而格上下矣。然豈無其本哉？仰惟
translation_en:
…purport. In elucidating the teaching of the Odes, bringing all under Heaven within the sovereign’s supreme standard, and following the distant tracks of the Three Hundred Odes, our emperor has in every respect grasped their profound essence and attained their purity. Thus, over the past twenty-four years, those who follow the Way have been greatly transformed, and those who behold the sage sovereign have been splendidly renewed. The subtle words of the Great Compendium shine forth like the sun and stars, while his immense grace and abundant beneficence equal Heaven and Earth. Here indeed we see how he accords with the two founding ancestors and carries forward the distant flourishing of the ages of Yao and Shun and the Three Dynasties. This is something the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song would never have dared aspire to. Yet you still earnestly condescend to ask me, wishing to sing of one or two aspects of this achievement and thereby proclaim the sage sovereign’s expansive and impartial transforming influence. What more can an ignorant man like me say?
The loyal and devoted ministers of antiquity strove to extol their ruler’s virtues, always seeking thereby to inspire all under Heaven and later generations, so that these virtues would become familiar to their ears, penetrate their hearts, and never be forgotten. Thus, in the flourishing days of the Zhou, with its multitude of worthy men, one ode said, “May the king of Zhou enjoy long life! Does he not nurture men of talent?” Another said, “The men of old were tireless in fostering these outstanding scholars.” Their purpose in singing of King Wen’s virtue was always to bring people to the supreme standard. Now our emperor personally acts as teacher and leader, instructing all under Heaven through the Odes. His influence has indeed already illuminated the four outer limits and reached above and below. Yet surely this has its foundation? Reverently considering…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
天縱之資獨超千古
日新之德遠邁百王首制
明倫大典一書推明統嗣之不同詳論義情
之兼盡則人極立而天下之綱常以定又
製爲
敬一之箴致謹於
郊廟天人之際益密於言行始終之常則
聖學煕而千聖之心法以傳由是以至道之凝
敷之於文則天下優游涵泳浹洽薫蒸而
===
歸于有極者孰不咏歌
聖明作人之澤於萬年也哉愚生躬逢
盛世竊伏海邦叨被
敎化有年矣思欲操觚翰以繪造化顧
廣大淵微有未易以形容者倘執事引而進之
尚當述天保鳧鷖之盛以揄揚其萬一不
敢諉於願學而未能也
第二問
邵型
punctuated:
天縱之資，獨超千古；日新之德，遠邁百王。首制《明倫大典》一書，推明統嗣之不同，詳論義情之兼盡，則人極立而天下之綱常以定。又製爲《敬一》之箴，致謹於郊廟天人之際，益密於言行始終之常，則聖學煕而千聖之心法以傳。由是以至道之凝，敷之於文，則天下優游涵泳，浹洽薫蒸，而歸于有極者，孰不咏歌聖明作人之澤於萬年也哉！愚生躬逢盛世，竊伏海邦，叨被敎化有年矣。思欲操觚翰以繪造化，顧廣大淵微，有未易以形容者。倘執事引而進之，尚當述《天保》《鳧鷖》之盛，以揄揚其萬一，不敢諉於願學而未能也。

第二問
邵型
translation_en:
…Your Majesty’s Heaven-endowed gifts uniquely surpass all antiquity; your virtue, renewed daily, far exceeds that of the hundred kings. You first composed the Great Compendium Clarifying Human Relations (Minglun dadian), elucidating the distinction between succession to the imperial line and succession as an heir, and explaining fully how both righteousness and familial feeling may be satisfied. Thus the supreme standard of human conduct was established, and the cardinal bonds and constant virtues of the realm were settled. You also composed the Admonition on Reverence and Unity (Jingyi), exercising care in the suburban and ancestral-temple sacrifices, where Heaven and humanity meet, and attending ever more closely to the constant standards governing words and deeds from beginning to end. Thus your sagely learning flourished, and the teachings of the mind handed down by all the sages were transmitted. From this concentration of the ultimate Way, you spread it through literary expression. All under Heaven dwell at ease within its influence, steeped in it and thoroughly imbued with it, and turn toward the supreme standard. Who among them would not sing for ten thousand years of the enlightened sage ruler’s beneficence in nurturing worthy men?

I, an unworthy scholar, have personally encountered this flourishing age. Dwelling obscurely in this coastal region, I have enjoyed your transforming instruction for many years. I wish to take up writing tablet and brush to portray this creative transformation; yet its breadth and depth, its profundity and subtlety, are not easily represented. If you, honored examiners, should guide me forward and advance me, I shall further recount the flourishing conditions celebrated in “Heaven Preserves You” (Tianbao) and “Wild Ducks and Gulls” (Fuyi), praising even a ten-thousandth part of your achievements. I dare not excuse myself by saying that I wish to learn but am not yet capable.

Second Question
Shao Xing

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
同考試官敎諭倪批律呂之法義理深奧子
能據實條陳辨析秋毫可以占該博之學矣
考試官學正馮批候氣以定律審音以知
樂此作敘述明確真知言哉
考試官學正劉批窮理之學
夫樂之用廣矣大矣所以同民心而出治
道者也然其作之也有本其正之也有法
政善民安天下太和此作樂之本也本自
然之氣以定律因一定之律以審音此正
===
樂之法也是故假音以宣和而不倚於音
也必求乎審音之法本和以作樂而不徒
爲和也必求乎致和之道則和以定律律
以審音比音而樂之以成樂以合天地以
和神人天下化中治於是乎成矣不狀音
爲乖戾之音而所謂和者非天地之太和
又何以作樂也哉執事發策詳究正樂之
法而終及馬遷律書之旨蓋以此也夫作
樂果有本乎樂云樂云鐘鼓云乎哉孔子
punctuated:
同考試官敎諭倪批：「律呂之法，義理深奧，子能據實條陳，辨析秋毫，可以占該博之學矣。」

考試官學正馮批：「候氣以定律，審音以知樂，此作敘述明確，真知言哉！」

考試官學正劉批：「窮理之學。」

夫樂之用廣矣，大矣，所以同民心而出治道者也。然其作之也有本，其正之也有法。政善民安，天下太和，此作樂之本也。本自然之氣以定律，因一定之律以審音，此正樂之法也。是故假音以宣和，而不倚於音也，必求乎審音之法；本和以作樂，而不徒爲和也，必求乎致和之道。則和以定律，律以審音，比音而樂之，以成樂，以合天地，以和神人，天下化中，治於是乎成矣。不狀音爲乖戾之音，而所謂和者非天地之太和，又何以作樂也哉？執事發策，詳究正樂之法，而終及馬遷《律書》之旨，蓋以此也。夫作樂果有本乎？「樂云樂云，鐘鼓云乎哉？」孔子
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Ni, Instructor, comments: “The principles underlying the pitch standards are profound and abstruse. You have set them out point by point on a factual basis and distinguished the finest details. This reveals the breadth of your learning.”

Examiner Feng, School Instructor, comments: “Observing qi to establish pitch standards, and examining tones to understand music: this essay gives a clear and precise account. These are truly words of understanding!”

Examiner Liu, School Instructor, comments: “Learning that probes principles to their utmost.”

The uses of music are broad and great indeed: it unites the hearts of the people and brings forth the Way of governance. Yet its creation has a foundation, and its rectification has a method. Good government, a people at peace, and supreme harmony throughout the world constitute the foundation for creating music. Establishing pitch standards on the basis of the qi of nature, and examining tones according to those fixed standards, constitute the method for rectifying music. Thus, although tones are employed to express harmony, one must not rely on tones alone: one must seek the method for examining them. Although music is created on the basis of harmony, one must not merely pursue harmony: one must seek the Way of bringing harmony about. Then harmony establishes pitch standards, and pitch standards serve to examine tones; tones are arranged and performed to produce music, to accord with Heaven and Earth, and to harmonize spirits and human beings. All under Heaven are transformed toward the mean, and good governance is thereby achieved. If the tones are discordant [?], and what is called harmony is not the supreme harmony of Heaven and Earth, how could music be created? Your policy question investigates in detail the method for rectifying music and concludes by addressing the purport of Sima Qian’s Treatise on the Pitch Standards; presumably this is the reason.

Does creating music indeed have a foundation? “Music, music! Does this mean merely bells and drums?” Confucius …

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
蓋嘗言之矣作樂抑有法乎聖人既竭耳
力焉繼之以六律正五音不可勝用也孟
子蓋嘗言之矣是二者之於樂雖有先後
緩急之殊要皆不可以偏廢焉者故知正
樂之法而不知其本固不可以成樂使知
正樂而不先求聲氣之元則雖斷竹鑄鐘
窮日夜之力以較其合否亦見其徒勞焉
耳嗚呼知此可與論樂矣愚也請先窮其
法而後及其本可乎蓋自黃帝命伶倫取
===
嶰谷之竹斷兩節而吹之以聽鳳凰之鳴
其雄鳴六者屬陽為律曰黃鐘太簇姑洗
蕤賓夷則亡射是也雌鳴六者屬陰為呂
曰大呂夾鐘仲呂林鐘南呂應鐘是也此
律呂之法所自起也然黃帝之律豈假物
而強制者哉蓋其垂衣裳而天下治至和
浹洽鳳鳥來鳴是為和氣之應故聽之以
制律班固所謂至治之世天地之氣合以
生風天地之風氣正則十二律定此之謂
punctuated: 蓋嘗言之矣。作樂抑有法乎？「聖人既竭耳力焉，繼之以六律，正五音，不可勝用也。」孟子蓋嘗言之矣。是二者之於樂，雖有先後緩急之殊，要皆不可以偏廢焉者。故知正樂之法而不知其本，固不可以成樂；使知正樂而不先求聲氣之元，則雖斷竹鑄鐘，窮日夜之力以較其合否，亦見其徒勞焉耳。嗚呼！知此，可與論樂矣。愚也請先窮其法而後及其本，可乎？蓋自黃帝命伶倫取嶰谷之竹，斷兩節而吹之，以聽鳳凰之鳴，其雄鳴六者屬陽為律，曰黃鐘、太簇、姑洗、蕤賓、夷則、亡射是也；雌鳴六者屬陰為呂，曰大呂、夾鐘、仲呂、林鐘、南呂、應鐘是也。此律呂之法所自起也。然黃帝之律，豈假物而強制者哉？蓋其垂衣裳而天下治，至和浹洽，鳳鳥來鳴，是為和氣之應，故聽之以制律。班固所謂「至治之世，天地之氣合以生風，天地之風氣正，則十二律定」，此之謂
translation_en:
…had indeed spoken of this. Yet are there also methods for making music? “The sage, having fully exerted his powers of hearing, followed this with the six pitch standards to rectify the five notes, making their use inexhaustible.” Mengzi indeed said this. Although these two aspects of music differ in precedence and urgency, neither may be neglected in favor of the other. Thus, knowing the methods for rectifying music without knowing its foundation certainly cannot bring music to completion. Even if one knows how to rectify music, unless one first seeks the source of sound and vital energy, then cutting bamboo and casting bells, laboring day and night to compare whether their pitches agree, will prove merely fruitless toil. Alas! With this understanding, one may discuss music. May I, in my humble ignorance, first investigate its methods fully and then address its foundation?

It began when Huangdi commanded Ling Lun to take bamboo from the Xie Valley, cut it at two joints, and blow it while listening to the calls of the phoenixes. The male’s six calls belonged to yang and constituted the six lü pitch standards: Huangzhong, Taicu, Guxian, Ruibin, Yize, and Wuyi. The female’s six calls belonged to yin and constituted the six complementary lü pitch standards: Dalü, Jiazhong, Zhonglü, Linzhong, Nanlü, and Yingzhong. This was the origin of the system of pitch standards. Yet were Huangdi’s pitch standards arbitrarily imposed by using external objects? Under his rule, he merely let his robes hang down, and the realm was well governed. Supreme harmony permeated everything, and phoenixes came and sang. This was a response to harmonious vital energy; hence he listened to them to establish the pitch standards. As Ban Gu said, “In an age of consummate governance, the vital energies of Heaven and Earth unite to produce wind. When the winds and vital energies of Heaven and Earth are properly ordered, the twelve pitch standards are established.” This is what is meant by…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
也是故論其名義則黃者中之色君之服
也鐘者種也陽氣生於黃泉孳萌萬物爲
六氣元也以黃色名元氣律者著宮聲也
大呂旅也蔟奏也夾助也姑辜也洗絜也
所以取其旅助黃鐘宣氣而生物者也仲
呂旅也蕤繼也賓導也林君也則法也南
任也射厭也應應也所以取其宣導陰氣
助陽而成物者也此十二律之名義也論
其起數則黃鐘之管長九十黍之廣積九
===
寸而度生焉容千二百黍積八百一十分
而量生焉重十有二銖而權衡生焉夫律
固可以制度量衡而考度量衡以一天下
之爭平天下之情聖人致和定律之本不
於是乎在耶論其測候則重室閉戶布以
緹縵實以葭灰按律候之以動之大小遲
速驗風氣之和否此候氣之法所由施也
夫律者陽氣之動陽聲之始必聲和氣應
然後可以見天地之心聖人順時正樂以
punctuated:
也。是故，論其名義，則黃者，中之色，君之服也；鐘者，種也，陽氣生於黃泉，孳萌萬物，爲六氣元也。以黃色名元氣律者，著宮聲也。大呂，旅也；蔟，奏也；夾，助也；姑，辜也；洗，絜也。所以取其旅助黃鐘，宣氣而生物者也。仲呂，旅也；蕤，繼也；賓，導也；林，君也；則，法也；南，任也；射，厭也；應，應也。所以取其宣導陰氣，助陽而成物者也。此十二律之名義也。
論其起數，則黃鐘之管長九十黍之廣，積九寸，而度生焉；容千二百黍，積八百一十分，而量生焉；重十有二銖，而權衡生焉。夫律固可以制度量衡，而考度量衡，以一天下之爭，平天下之情。聖人致和定律之本，不於是乎在耶？
論其測候，則重室閉戶，布以緹縵，實以葭灰，按律候之，以動之大小遲速，驗風氣之和否。此候氣之法所由施也。夫律者，陽氣之動，陽聲之始，必聲和氣應，然後可以見天地之心。聖人順時正樂以
translation_en:
… Thus, to discuss the meanings of their names: huang, “yellow,” is the color of the center and the color of the ruler’s robes. Zhong, “bell,” means “seed”: yang qi arises in the Yellow Springs beneath the earth and germinates the myriad things, serving as the origin of the six qi. Naming the pitch standard of primordial qi after the color yellow makes manifest the gong tone. In Dalu, lu means “array”; cu means “perform”; jia means “assist”; gu means “fault” [?]; and xian means “cleanse.” These meanings are adopted to express their arraying themselves to assist Huangzhong, disseminating qi and bringing things to life. In Zhonglu, lu means “array”; rui means “continue”; bin means “guide”; lin means “ruler”; ze means “rule”; nan means “bear”; yi means “satiate”; and ying means “respond.” These meanings are adopted to express their disseminating and guiding yin qi, assisting yang and bringing things to completion. Such are the meanings of the names of the twelve pitch standards.
To discuss the derivation of their numerical measures: the Huangzhong pitch pipe is ninety millet-grain breadths long, amounting to nine cun; from this arises the standard of length. It holds twelve hundred millet grains, amounting to eight hundred and ten fen of volume; from this arises the standard of capacity. Their weight is twelve zhu; from this arise weights and balances. Pitch standards can indeed establish measures of length, capacity, and weight. By checking these measures, one can settle disputes throughout the realm and bring equity to people’s dealings. Does not the fundamental purpose of the sages in bringing about harmony and fixing pitch standards lie here?
To discuss their use in observation: within a chamber enclosed by another chamber, the doors are shut, reddish silk gauze is spread out, and the pitch pipes are filled with reed-membrane ash. Observations are made according to the pitch standards; the extent and speed of the ash’s movement are used to test whether the winds and qi are harmonious. This is how the method of observing qi is put into practice. Pitch standards embody the stirring of yang qi and the beginning of yang sound. Only when sound is harmonious and qi responds can the heart of Heaven and Earth be perceived. The sages follow the seasons and rectify music in order to…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
合天地者不於是乎在耶至於律之所謂
上生下生者蓋先王因天地陰陽之氣辨
十有二辰而生十有二律其長短有度損
益有宜以陽律起數以陰律成之每三分
而損益隔八位而相生所謂娶妻生子之
說其理深矣故黃鐘損一下生林鐘林鐘
益一上生太簇循是相生至於仲呂以成
一終而所以損陽生陰益陰生陽之數無
不備焉此比次降殺之序乃陰陽消長之
===
機非巧筭者所能爲也其所謂旋相爲宮
者蓋十二律所以配十二月各有用事之
辰故得旋相爲宮然多寡有數輕重有權
以正變相運而以減半節之使黃鐘有常
尊諸律不得以相凌所謂同心一統之義
其理微矣故黃鐘爲宮則林鐘諸律以次
而應之以全分之正聲林鐘爲宮則太簇
諸律以次而應之以減半之子聲此尊卑
隆殺之法天地自然之分非拘執者所能
punctuated:
合天地者，不於是乎在耶？至於律之所謂上生下生者，蓋先王因天地陰陽之氣，辨十有二辰而生十有二律。其長短有度，損益有宜，以陽律起數，以陰律成之。每三分而損益，隔八位而相生，所謂娶妻生子之說，其理深矣。故黃鐘損一下生林鐘，林鐘益一上生太簇，循是相生，至於仲呂，以成一終，而所以損陽生陰、益陰生陽之數，無不備焉。此比次降殺之序，乃陰陽消長之機，非巧筭者所能爲也。

其所謂旋相爲宮者，蓋十二律所以配十二月，各有用事之辰，故得旋相爲宮。然多寡有數，輕重有權，以正變相運，而以減半節之，使黃鐘有常尊，諸律不得以相凌。所謂同心一統之義，其理微矣。故黃鐘爲宮，則林鐘諸律以次而應之，以全分之正聲；林鐘爲宮，則太簇諸律以次而應之，以減半之子聲。此尊卑隆殺之法，天地自然之分，非拘執者所能
translation_en:
…to accord with Heaven and Earth—is this not where its basis lies? As for what pitch theory calls “upward generation” and “downward generation,” the former kings followed the qi of Heaven and Earth, yin and yang, distinguishing the twelve stations and generating the twelve pitch standards. Their lengths have prescribed measures, and their reductions and augmentations are appropriately regulated. The numerical sequence begins with a yang pitch standard and is completed through a yin pitch standard. At each step, the length is divided into thirds and reduced or augmented by one third; the pitch standards generate one another at intervals of eight positions. The principle behind the so-called “taking a wife and begetting a son” is profound indeed. Thus Huangzhong, reduced by one third, generates Linzhong downward; Linzhong, augmented by one third, generates Taicu upward. Generation continues in this way until Zhonglü is reached, completing one cycle. All the numerical operations by which yang is reduced to generate yin and yin is augmented to generate yang are thereby fully encompassed. This ordered sequence of gradations and reductions is the mechanism of yin and yang waxing and waning; it is not something that clever calculators could contrive.

As for what is called “serving in turn as gong,” the twelve pitch standards correspond to the twelve months, each having its own time of ascendancy; hence each can serve in turn as gong, the principal scale tone. Yet greater and lesser quantities have their numerical rules, and lighter and heavier weights their standards of balance. The regular and altered tones operate together, regulated by halving, so that Huangzhong retains its constant supremacy and the other pitch standards cannot encroach upon one another. The principle behind what is called “being of one mind under a single rule” is subtle indeed. Thus, when Huangzhong serves as gong, Linzhong and the other pitch standards respond to it in sequence with the regular tones of their full lengths; when Linzhong serves as gong, Taicu and the other pitch standards respond to it in sequence with the subsidiary tones of their halved lengths. This method of ordering higher and lower ranks, elevation and diminution, embodies the natural distinctions of Heaven and Earth; it is not something that those bound by rigid preconceptions can…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
成也凡此皆先王正樂之法自黃帝以來
三代因之而不改者也秦火以後樂書散
亡古制隨失司馬遷拾三代之遺文以著
律書其所載十二律分寸之數相生之法
雖略而未詳然去古未遠大率皆聖人之
遺也但其始也不言律而言兵不言兵之
用而言兵之偃者其故何哉蓋以聖人作
樂必本於大和致和之道必由於安百姓
百姓之安樂必由於休兵而息民故其言
===
曰文帝之時能不擾亂由是天下富庶雞
鳴犬吠煙火萬里百姓遂安嗚呼若太史
公者可謂達制律之意知作樂之本者矣
先儒陳氏稱之曰律呂之法起於黃帝律
呂之說定於太史公不其然乎哉嗣是京
房得焦延壽之傳擬六十四卦之義而為
六十律相生之法其說比司馬為詳然陽
必下生陰必上生無比次降殺之序非聖
人損益相生之本意其法已不可與馬遷
punctuated:
成也。凡此皆先王正樂之法，自黃帝以來，三代因之而不改者也。秦火以後，樂書散亡，古制隨失。司馬遷拾三代之遺文以著《律書》，其所載十二律分寸之數、相生之法，雖略而未詳，然去古未遠，大率皆聖人之遺也。但其始也，不言律而言兵，不言兵之用而言兵之偃者，其故何哉？蓋以聖人作樂，必本於大和；致和之道，必由於安百姓；百姓之安樂，必由於休兵而息民。故其言曰：「文帝之時，能不擾亂，由是天下富庶，雞鳴犬吠，煙火萬里，百姓遂安。」嗚呼！若太史公者，可謂達制律之意、知作樂之本者矣。先儒陳氏稱之曰：「律呂之法起於黃帝，律呂之說定於太史公。」不其然乎哉？
嗣是，京房得焦延壽之傳，擬六十四卦之義而為六十律相生之法。其說比司馬為詳，然陽必下生，陰必上生，無比次降殺之序，非聖人損益相生之本意，其法已不可與馬遷
translation_en:
…accomplish. All these are the former kings’ methods for putting music in proper order. Originating with the Yellow Emperor, they were followed without alteration throughout the Three Dynasties. After the Qin burning of books, writings on music were scattered and lost, and the ancient institutions disappeared along with them. Sima Qian gathered surviving writings from the Three Dynasties to compose his Treatise on the Pitch Standards (Lü shu). Its account of the lengths of the twelve pitch pipes in fen and cun, and of the method by which they generate one another, is brief and lacks detail. Yet his time was not far removed from antiquity, and these were, for the most part, teachings bequeathed by the sages. But why does he begin by discussing warfare rather than pitch standards, and the cessation of warfare rather than the use of arms? It is because the sages necessarily grounded the creation of music in supreme harmony. The way to bring about harmony necessarily proceeds through bringing peace to the common people; their peace and happiness necessarily depend on ending warfare and allowing them rest. Thus he says: “In Emperor Wen’s time, he was able to refrain from disturbing the people. Consequently, all under Heaven grew prosperous and populous; cocks crowed and dogs barked, smoke rose from hearths for ten thousand li, and the common people attained peace.” Ah! A man such as the Grand Astrologer may indeed be said to have understood the intent behind establishing pitch standards and known the foundation of creating music. The earlier Confucian scholar Chen praised him, saying: “The methods of the pitch standards originated with the Yellow Emperor; their exposition was definitively established by the Grand Astrologer.” Is this not indeed so?
Subsequently, Jing Fang received the teachings transmitted by Jiao Yanshou and, taking the principles of the sixty-four hexagrams as his model, devised a method by which sixty pitch standards generate one another. His exposition is more detailed than Sima Qian’s. Yet in it, yang must always generate downward and yin must always generate upward, without an ordered sequence of successive gradations and reductions. This was not the sages’ original intention in having pitches generate one another through diminution and augmentation. His method already cannot be placed alongside that of Sima Qian…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
同矣况元帝何時而汲汲於言律以審音
哉逮宋元嘉中太史錢樂之又以京房六
十律相生之法更生三百律以當三百六
十之策其法視京房爲益詳然相生之法
猶夫房也安得與古制同乎矧元嘉之時
比元帝又遠矣夫聖王制律必求聲氣之
元故太史公曰細若氣微若聲聖人因神
而存之雖妙必效言黃鐘始於聲氣之元
非律生於黍也而漢志隋書及房庶之徒
===
乃以古人皆累黍爲尺以制律而爲縱橫
長短之說其謬已甚若乃易竹用銅取其
同天下之風俗以準代竹取其審聲音之
易達似有益於樂者然亦後代之制非古
先王之法也以至阮咸荀勗之徒雖負神
解暗解之名類恃器數之末而不求聲氣
之元已不得定律之法而况望其識制律
之意如馬遷乎宋范鎮曰樂者和氣也發
和氣者聲音也古人以有形之物傳其法
punctuated: 同矣，况元帝何時，而汲汲於言律以審音哉？逮宋元嘉中，太史錢樂之又以京房六十律相生之法，更生三百律，以當三百六十之策。其法視京房爲益詳，然相生之法猶夫房也，安得與古制同乎？矧元嘉之時，比元帝又遠矣！夫聖王制律，必求聲氣之元。故太史公曰：「細若氣，微若聲，聖人因神而存之，雖妙必效。」言黃鐘始於聲氣之元，非律生於黍也。而漢志、隋書及房庶之徒，乃以古人皆累黍爲尺以制律，而爲縱橫長短之說，其謬已甚。若乃易竹用銅，取其同天下之風俗；以準代竹，取其審聲音之易達，似有益於樂者。然亦後代之制，非古先王之法也。以至阮咸、荀勗之徒，雖負神解、暗解之名，類恃器數之末，而不求聲氣之元，已不得定律之法，而况望其識制律之意如馬遷乎？宋范鎮曰：「樂者，和氣也；發和氣者，聲音也。古人以有形之物傳其法
translation_en:
…be considered the same. Moreover, what sort of age was that of Emperor Yuan of Han, that he should have been so intent on discussing pitch standards to ascertain musical tones? During the Yuanjia reign of the Liu Song dynasty, the Grand Astrologer Qian Lezhi again used Jing Fang’s method of successively generating sixty pitch standards to generate three hundred more, corresponding to the three hundred and sixty divination stalks. His method was more elaborate than Jing Fang’s, but its procedure for generating pitches remained Jing Fang’s. How could it agree with the ancient system? Furthermore, the Yuanjia era was even more remote from antiquity than Emperor Yuan’s time!

When the sage kings established pitch standards, they invariably sought the source of sound and qi. Thus the Grand Historian said: “Fine as qi, subtle as sound: the sage follows its numinous workings and preserves it; though mysterious, it must produce verifiable effects.” This means that the Yellow Bell pitch originates in the source of sound and qi, rather than that pitch standards originate in millet grains. Yet the treatise in the History of Han, the History of Sui, and men such as Fang Shu held that the ancients all made their measuring rules by lining up millet grains in order to establish pitch standards. They consequently advanced theories about arranging the grains lengthwise or crosswise and about the resulting lengths. Their error was already very great.

As for replacing bamboo with bronze, this was adopted to unify customs throughout the realm; replacing bamboo with the tuning instrument called the zhun was adopted because it made the determination of musical tones readily comprehensible. These measures seem to have benefited music. Nevertheless, they too were institutions of later ages, not the methods of the ancient kings. Even men such as Ruan Xian and Xun Xu, though renowned for their inspired or intuitive understanding, generally relied on the secondary details of instruments and numerical relationships without seeking the source of sound and qi. They thus failed even to grasp the method of determining pitch standards. How much less could one expect them to understand the intent behind establishing those standards as Sima Qian did?

Fan Zhen of the Song said: “Music is harmonious qi; what gives expression to harmonious qi is sound. The ancients transmitted their methods through tangible objects…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
然後無形之聲音得而和氣可道有形者
秬黍也律也尺也龠也鬴也斛也筭數也
權衡也鐘也磬也是十物者必相合而不
相戾然後為得而馬遷律書率所不載蓋
器數之末非正樂之本聲氣之元不得則
黃鐘之律不定所謂十物者特虛器耳欲
求相合而不相戾也得乎故制律者必先
求聲氣之元以定黃鐘之管然後十二律
定而和氣可道此正樂之法不可易者舍
===
是言樂亦末矣雖然此法也非本也記曰
凡音者生人心者也治世之音安以樂其
政和聲音之道與政通矣是故政善則民
安民安則心和心和則氣和氣和則形和
形和則聲和聲和則天地之和應之即愚
所謂百姓安樂天下大和如律書之旨是
也猶未也記又曰音者生於人心者也樂
者通倫理者也不知聲者不可與言音不
知音者不可與言樂知樂則幾於禮矣禮
punctuated:
然後無形之聲音得，而和氣可道。有形者，秬黍也，律也，尺也，龠也，鬴也，斛也，筭數也，權衡也，鐘也，磬也。是十物者，必相合而不相戾，然後為得。」而馬遷《律書》率所不載，蓋器數之末，非正樂之本。聲氣之元不得，則黃鐘之律不定，所謂十物者特虛器耳。欲求相合而不相戾也，得乎？故制律者必先求聲氣之元，以定黃鐘之管，然後十二律定，而和氣可道。此正樂之法不可易者，舍是言樂，亦末矣。
雖然，此法也，非本也。《記》曰：「凡音者，生人心者也。治世之音安以樂，其政和。」聲音之道，與政通矣。是故政善則民安，民安則心和，心和則氣和，氣和則形和，形和則聲和，聲和則天地之和應之。即愚所謂百姓安樂，天下大和，如《律書》之旨是也。猶未也。《記》又曰：「音者，生於人心者也。樂者，通倫理者也。不知聲者，不可與言音；不知音者，不可與言樂。知樂則幾於禮矣。禮
translation_en:
…only then can formless sounds be correctly obtained and harmonious qi be brought forth. The tangible things are black millet, pitch standards, measuring rules, yue measures, fu measures, hu measures, numerical calculations, weights and balances, bells, and sounding stones. These ten things must agree with one another and not conflict; only then is correctness attained.” Yet these are generally not recorded in Sima Qian’s Treatise on Pitch Standards. They are, after all, the subsidiary details of instruments and numbers, rather than the foundation for rectifying music. Unless the source of sound and qi is apprehended, the pitch standard of Huangzhong cannot be fixed, and the so-called ten things are merely empty apparatus. Could one then hope to make them agree without conflict? Thus, those who establish pitch standards must first seek the source of sound and qi in order to fix the Huangzhong pitch pipe. Only then can the twelve pitch standards be fixed and harmonious qi be brought forth. This is the unalterable method for rectifying music. To discuss music while abandoning it is likewise to concern oneself with mere incidentals.
Nevertheless, this is a method, not the foundation. The Book of Rites says: “All musical tones arise from the human heart. The tones of a well-governed age are peaceful and joyous, for its government is harmonious.” The way of sounds and tones is interconnected with government. Thus, when government is good, the people are at peace; when the people are at peace, their hearts are harmonious; when their hearts are harmonious, their qi is harmonious; when their qi is harmonious, their bodily forms are harmonious; when their bodily forms are harmonious, their voices are harmonious; and when their voices are harmonious, the harmony of Heaven and Earth responds to them. This is precisely what I, in my humble view, mean by the people being peaceful and happy and all under Heaven enjoying great harmony, in keeping with the purport of the Treatise on Pitch Standards. Yet this is still not all. The Book of Rites also says: “Musical tones arise from the human heart. Music brings ethical relationships into mutual accord. With someone who does not understand sounds, one cannot discuss tones; with someone who does not understand tones, one cannot discuss music. To understand music is to come close to understanding ritual. Ritual …

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
樂皆得謂之有德此禮樂合一之說作樂
者又不可以不察也然樂豈易作哉自兩
漢以降其間英君誼辟相與向慕而講求
不啻聚訟而卒未有能復古樂者凡以不
得其本焉耳於乎契天地之心建中和之
極使大和之治洋溢於天下以追咸英韶
濩之風愚何幸有見於
今日
第叁問
===
汪梯
同考試官教諭廖 批 化工天地之糟粕經史
聖人之緒餘後之儒者漸益爲經爲史亦贅矣此
策能詳言之謂究心於經史之精者非耶
同考試官教諭劉 批 博洽之才
同考試官教諭張 批 擬議精當迥異諸作
考試官學正馮 批 明經可以治史明史可
以翼經是篇有考據有斷制宜錄以式來學
考試官學正劉 批 詞閎學贍
punctuated:
樂皆得，謂之有德。此禮樂合一之說，作樂者又不可以不察也。然樂豈易作哉？自兩漢以降，其間英君誼辟，相與向慕而講求，不啻聚訟，而卒未有能復古樂者，凡以不得其本焉耳。於乎！契天地之心，建中和之極，使大和之治洋溢於天下，以追咸英韶濩之風，愚何幸有見於今日！
第叁問
汪梯
同考試官教諭廖批：化工，天地之糟粕；經史，聖人之緒餘。後之儒者漸益爲經爲史，亦贅矣。此策能詳言之，謂究心於經史之精者，非耶？
同考試官教諭劉批：博洽之才。
同考試官教諭張批：擬議精當，迥異諸作。
考試官學正馮批：明經可以治史，明史可以翼經。是篇有考據，有斷制，宜錄以式來學。
考試官學正劉批：詞閎學贍。
translation_en:
…when both rites and music are mastered, this is called possessing virtue. This explanation of the unity of rites and music is something that those who create music must also examine. Yet how could music be easy to create? From the two Han dynasties onward, outstanding rulers and righteous sovereigns alike admired and sought it, investigating and debating it in seemingly endless disputes. Yet ultimately none could restore ancient music, simply because they failed to grasp its foundation. Ah! To accord with the heart of Heaven and Earth, establish the supreme standard of centrality and harmony, and cause a reign of great harmony to overflow throughout the realm, thereby recapturing the spirit of the ancient music of Xian, Ying, Shao, and Huo—how fortunate I am to witness this today!
Third Question
Wang Ti 汪梯
Comment by Associate Examiner Liao, Instructor: “The work of creation is the dregs of Heaven and Earth; the classics and histories are the remnants left by the sages. Later scholars have gradually added to these, producing classics and histories: this, too, is superfluous. This policy essay explains the matter in detail. Would it not be right to call its author someone who has devoted his mind to the essential meaning of the classics and histories?”
Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: “A talent of broad and comprehensive learning.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: “His deliberations are precise and apt, markedly different from the other compositions.”
Comment by Examiner Feng, School Instructor: “Understanding the classics enables one to study history; understanding history enables one to supplement the classics. This essay offers both examination of evidence and decisive judgments. It should be recorded as a model for future students.”
Comment by Examiner Liu, School Instructor: “Expansive language and abundant learning.”

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
蓋聞天下之道一也所以闡而明之者經
史而已矣夫經者非飾辭也體天人之撰
至精而不易者道之準也史者非備事也
持是非之衡至變而有則者道之紀也窮
經而不以道則無以極其精考史而不以
道則無以盡其變而其學也亦徒矣知此
則經史不同同歸於道固聖賢所以維世
教淑人心者也是可以泛求乎哉且鴻濛
旣判書契巳傳木繩棄而不行文籍於是
===
===
乎興矣而古今載籍之大孰有過於經史
者乎然經以載道聖賢傳心之要典史以
紀事史官一代之實錄若是乎其不侔也
及觀蘇洵謂經與史其義一其體二王通
謂聖人述史有三書詩春秋同出於史而
不可離則經與史豈各自為義者乎是故
經以道法勝矣若典謨訓誥諸篇詳于政
事即經中之史也史以事辭勝矣若朱熹
綱目謹于名分即史中之經也則經與史
punctuated: 蓋聞天下之道一也，所以闡而明之者，經史而已矣。夫經者，非飾辭也；體天人之撰，至精而不易者，道之準也。史者，非備事也；持是非之衡，至變而有則者，道之紀也。窮經而不以道，則無以極其精；考史而不以道，則無以盡其變，而其學也亦徒矣。知此，則經史不同，同歸於道，固聖賢所以維世教、淑人心者也。是可以泛求乎哉？且鴻濛旣判，書契巳傳，木繩棄而不行，文籍於是乎興矣。而古今載籍之大，孰有過於經史者乎？然經以載道，聖賢傳心之要典；史以紀事，史官一代之實錄。若是乎其不侔也！及觀蘇洵謂經與史其義一、其體二，王通謂聖人述史有三：《書》、《詩》、《春秋》，同出於史而不可離，則經與史豈各自為義者乎？是故經以道法勝矣，若典謨訓誥諸篇詳于政事，即經中之史也；史以事辭勝矣，若朱熹《綱目》謹于名分，即史中之經也。則經與史
translation_en:
I have heard that the Way under Heaven is one, and that what expounds and elucidates it consists simply of the classics and histories. The classics are not embellishments of language: embodying the workings of Heaven and humanity, supremely refined and unchanging, they are the standard of the Way. The histories are not merely comprehensive records of events: holding the balance of right and wrong, encompassing the utmost change yet governed by principles, they are the guiding framework of the Way. If one investigates the classics without taking the Way as one’s basis, one cannot fathom their subtlety; if one examines the histories without taking the Way as one’s basis, one cannot fully comprehend their changes. Such learning is futile. Once this is understood, it becomes clear that, although the classics and histories differ, both converge upon the Way. They are indeed the means by which sages and worthies sustain moral instruction in the world and improve people’s hearts. Can they be approached superficially?

Once primordial chaos had divided and writing had been transmitted, wooden tallies and knotted cords [?] were abandoned and ceased to be used; written records then arose. Among the great bodies of writing, ancient and modern, what surpasses the classics and histories? Yet the classics convey the Way and are the essential canons through which sages and worthies transmit their understanding; the histories record events and are the historiographers’ veritable records of a dynasty. How different they seem! But consider Su Xun’s statement that the classics and histories are one in meaning but two in form, and Wang Tong’s statement that the sage’s historical writings comprise three works—the Book of Documents, the Book of Odes, and the Spring and Autumn Annals—all deriving from history and inseparable from it. Can the classics and histories, then, each have a meaning entirely their own? Thus, the classics excel in the Way and its principles; nevertheless, such chapters as the Canons, Counsels, Instructions, and Announcements give detailed accounts of government affairs and constitute history within the classics. The histories excel in events and their narration; nevertheless, a work such as Zhu Xi’s Outline and Details (Gangmu), scrupulous about proper titles and status, constitutes a classic within history. Thus the classics and histories…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
非互爲用者乎惟其義一是以用同用同
矣又何論其體之異哉且易書詩春秋禮
樂世所謂六經也後乃漸益其數至於十
三經者抑何經之多耶蓋伏羲堯舜文王
周公陳卦辭敘典謨采歌謠明節奏而羣
經始備至孔子則又贊易以黜誕定禮樂
以黜僭刪詩書以黜不雅脩春秋以黜不
王而六經始明自秦人焚棄而樂亡謂之
五經禮分爲三謂之七經加以孝經論語
===
謂之九經春秋分三傳合孝經論語爲一
則爲十經以六經加六緯則爲十二經而
十三經者又以三禮三傳加孝經論孟爾
雅言也然三禮備成周致治之迹三傳述
聖人筆削之情孝經陳先王至德之要論
孟記鄒魯授受之言皆足以維持世道羽
翼六經者也若六緯燬于煬帝書多不存
爾雅注于景純文皆無緒惡可與諸經並
列哉然則經之要者莫如五經而孝經論
punctuated: 非互爲用者乎？惟其義一，是以用同。用同矣，又何論其體之異哉？且《易》《書》《詩》《春秋》《禮》《樂》，世所謂六經也。後乃漸益其數，至於十三經者，抑何經之多耶？蓋伏羲、堯、舜、文王、周公，陳卦辭，敘典謨，采歌謠，明節奏，而羣經始備。至孔子，則又贊《易》以黜誕，定禮樂以黜僭，刪《詩》《書》以黜不雅，脩《春秋》以黜不王，而六經始明。自秦人焚棄而《樂》亡，謂之五經；《禮》分爲三，謂之七經；加以《孝經》《論語》，謂之九經；《春秋》分三傳，合《孝經》《論語》爲一，則爲十經；以六經加六緯，則爲十二經。而十三經者，又以三禮、三傳，加《孝經》、論孟、《爾雅》言也。然三禮備成周致治之迹，三傳述聖人筆削之情，《孝經》陳先王至德之要，論孟記鄒魯授受之言，皆足以維持世道、羽翼六經者也。若六緯燬于煬帝，書多不存；《爾雅》注于景純，文皆無緒，惡可與諸經並列哉？然則經之要者莫如五經，而《孝經》、論
translation_en:
…do they not serve one another? Precisely because their meaning is one, their function is the same. Since their function is the same, why dwell on differences in their form? The Changes, Documents, Odes, Spring and Autumn Annals, Rites, and Music are what the world calls the Six Classics. Later their number gradually increased until there were Thirteen Classics. Why were there so many? Fuxi, Yao, Shun, King Wen, and the Duke of Zhou set forth the hexagram statements, arranged the canons and counsels, collected songs and ballads, and clarified musical rhythms; only then was the body of classics complete. When Confucius came, he further elucidated the Changes to exclude the fanciful, established rites and music to exclude usurpation, edited the Odes and Documents to exclude the unrefined, and revised the Spring and Autumn Annals to exclude departures from the kingly way. Only then were the Six Classics made clear. After the men of Qin burned and discarded them, the Music was lost, and they were called the Five Classics. When the Rites was divided into three, they were called the Seven Classics; with the addition of the Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects, they were called the Nine Classics. When the Spring and Autumn Annals was divided into three commentaries, and the Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects were counted as one, there were Ten Classics. Adding the six apocryphal texts to the Six Classics made Twelve Classics. As for the Thirteen Classics, this designation likewise counts the Three Ritual Classics and the Three Commentaries, together with the Classic of Filial Piety, the Analects, the Mencius, and the Erya, or Approaching Correct Usage.

The Three Ritual Classics fully preserve the traces of how good government was achieved under the Zhou; the Three Commentaries recount the sage’s intentions in recording and deleting; the Classic of Filial Piety sets forth the essentials of the former kings’ highest virtue; and the Analects and Mencius record the teachings transmitted and received in Zou and Lu. All are sufficient to sustain the moral order of the world and support the Six Classics. But the six apocryphal texts were destroyed under Emperor Yang, and much of their content no longer survives; the Erya was annotated by Jingchun, but its text is entirely without an organizing thread. How could these be ranked alongside the other classics? Thus, among the classics, none are more essential than the Five Classics, while the Classic of Filial Piety, the Analects…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
孟三禮三傳皆不可缺一者矣左傳公羊
穀梁世所謂三史也後乃漸益其數至於
二十一史者抑何史之多耶蓋史記而下
有兩漢書三國志而晉宋齊梁陳後魏北
齊後周莫不有書南北史而下有隋書唐
書而五代宋遼金元莫不有史自劉羲叟
爲宋著作郎編十二代史東萊呂氏乃增
定爲十七史雙湖胡氏亦有十七史纂廬
陵曾氏加爲十八史後加石門梁氏元史
===
略爲十九史而二十一史者則自漢至元
兼統其全言也觀夫史記之疎爽質直西
漢書之詳贍密塞東漢書之奇變不窮五
代史之善法春秋皆足以攷證世道不愧
名史者也若夫陳壽乞米之私魏收黷貨
之傳沈約琅琊之誣蕭子顯圖讖之紀惡
可與諸史並論哉然則史之善者莫如三
史而遷固范歐猶爲彼善于此者矣是故
經不必同于史也取其述性命闡彝倫可
punctuated:
孟、三禮、三傳，皆不可缺一者矣。《左傳》、《公羊》、《穀梁》，世所謂三史也。後乃漸益其數，至於二十一史者，抑何史之多耶？蓋《史記》而下，有兩《漢書》、《三國志》，而晉、宋、齊、梁、陳、後魏、北齊、後周，莫不有書。《南北史》而下，有《隋書》、《唐書》，而五代、宋、遼、金、元，莫不有史。自劉羲叟爲宋著作郎，編十二代史，東萊呂氏乃增定爲十七史，雙湖胡氏亦有《十七史纂》，廬陵曾氏加爲十八史，後加石門梁氏《元史略》，爲十九史。而二十一史者，則自漢至元，兼統其全言也。觀夫《史記》之疎爽質直，《西漢書》之詳贍密塞，《東漢書》之奇變不窮，《五代史》之善法《春秋》，皆足以攷證世道，不愧名史者也。若夫陳壽乞米之私、魏收黷貨之傳、沈約琅琊之誣、蕭子顯圖讖之紀，惡可與諸史並論哉？然則史之善者，莫如三史，而遷、固、范、歐，猶爲彼善于此者矣。
是故經不必同于史也，取其述性命、闡彝倫，可
translation_en:
…the Mencius, the Three Ritual Classics, and the Three Commentaries: not one of these can be dispensed with. The Zuo Commentary, the Gongyang Commentary, and the Guliang Commentary are what people commonly call the Three Histories. Later their number gradually increased, reaching twenty-one histories. Why should there be so many histories? After the Records of the Grand Historian came the two Books of Han and the Records of the Three Kingdoms; and Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, Chen, Later Wei, Northern Qi, and Later Zhou each had its own book. After the Histories of the Northern and Southern Dynasties came the Book of Sui and the Book of Tang; and the Five Dynasties, Song, Liao, Jin, and Yuan each had its own history. Liu Xisou, serving as Editorial Director under the Song, compiled the histories of twelve dynasties. Master Lü of Donglai then expanded and revised this collection to form the Seventeen Histories. Master Hu of Shuanghu also produced a Compilation of the Seventeen Histories. Master Zeng of Luling enlarged the collection to eighteen histories; subsequently, the Outline History of the Yuan by Master Liang of Shimen was added, making nineteen histories. The designation Twenty-One Histories, however, refers collectively to the complete set from Han to Yuan.
Consider the openness, clarity, simplicity, and directness of the Records of the Grand Historian; the detail, richness, density, and fullness of the Book of Western Han; the endlessly surprising variety of the Book of Eastern Han; and the skill with which the History of the Five Dynasties follows the example of the Spring and Autumn Annals. All are sufficient for examining and verifying the course of human affairs, and fully deserve the name of histories. But as for Chen Shou’s self-serving solicitation of rice, Wei Shou’s biographies tainted by bribery, Shen Yue’s false allegation concerning Langya [?], and Xiao Zixian’s recording of prophetic charts and prognostications—how could these be discussed on equal terms with the other histories? Thus, among the finest histories, none surpass the Three Histories; yet even among Sima Qian, Ban Gu, Fan Ye, and Ouyang Xiu, one may still be better than another.
Therefore, the classics need not be the same as the histories. What we draw from them is their exposition of human nature and destiny and their elucidation of the enduring human relationships, by which one may…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
以折衷諸史而不離乎散殊之迹史不必
同于經也取其注言動公是非可以羽翼
羣經而不悖乎精微之奧則經史之體雖
殊而學之者可以異求乎哉故欲窮經者
不必索之高深也惟在崇五敎而辨三岐
焉何謂五敎經解曰溫柔敦厚詩敎也疏
通知遠書敎也絜靜精微易敎也恭儉莊
敬禮敎也屬詞比事春秋敎也於是崇之
則能達經之原矣何謂三岐朱子論蘇軾
===
陳少南因文說理爲文人之經張子韶輩
語涉空幻爲禪者之經濂洛諸子承傳有
自爲儒者之經是也於是辨之則不戾經
之㫖矣若夫書叙六府曰水火金木土穀
是五行爲府也皇極經世則以四時四經
分配言之曰昊天之四府者春夏秋冬之
謂也陰陽升降于其間矣聖人之四府者
易書詩春秋之謂也禮樂隆汙于其間矣
蓋天時聖經相因而成盡物盡民不出四
punctuated:
以折衷諸史，而不離乎散殊之迹。史不必同于經也，取其注言動、公是非，可以羽翼羣經，而不悖乎精微之奧。則經史之體雖殊，而學之者可以異求乎哉？故欲窮經者，不必索之高深也，惟在崇五敎而辨三岐焉。何謂五敎？《經解》曰：「溫柔敦厚，詩敎也；疏通知遠，書敎也；絜靜精微，易敎也；恭儉莊敬，禮敎也；屬詞比事，春秋敎也。」於是崇之，則能達經之原矣。何謂三岐？朱子論蘇軾、陳少南因文說理，爲文人之經；張子韶輩語涉空幻，爲禪者之經；濂洛諸子承傳有自，爲儒者之經，是也。於是辨之，則不戾經之㫖矣。

若夫《書》叙六府，曰水、火、金、木、土、穀，是五行爲府也。《皇極經世》則以四時、四經分配言之，曰：「昊天之四府者，春夏秋冬之謂也，陰陽升降于其間矣；聖人之四府者，易、書、詩、春秋之謂也，禮樂隆汙于其間矣。」蓋天時、聖經相因而成，盡物盡民，不出四
translation_en:
…thereby adjudicating among the histories without departing from the traces of particular events. Histories need not be identical with the Classics: what we value in them is their recording of words and deeds and their impartial judgment of right and wrong. They can thus support the Classics without contradicting their subtle and profound meanings. Although the Classics and histories differ in form, then, can those who study them pursue different ends? Those who wish to fathom the Classics need not seek in lofty obscurities; they need only honor the five teachings and distinguish the three paths. What are the five teachings? “Explanation of the Classics” says: “Gentleness and sincerity are the teaching of the Odes; breadth of understanding and knowledge of the distant past are the teaching of the Documents; purity, tranquility, and subtle discernment are the teaching of the Changes; respectfulness, frugality, dignity, and reverence are the teaching of the Rites; arranging words and correlating events are the teaching of the Spring and Autumn Annals.” By honoring these, one can reach the source of the Classics. What are the three paths? Master Zhu described the interpretations of Su Shi and Chen Shaonan, who expounded principles through literary composition, as the Classics of literary men; those of Zhang Zishao and his fellows, whose language touched on emptiness and illusion, as the Classics of Chan Buddhists; and those of the masters of Lian and Luo, whose inherited teachings had an established source, as the Classics of Confucian scholars. These are the three paths. By distinguishing them, one will not depart from the purport of the Classics.

Now, the Documents enumerates the six treasuries as water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain: thus the five agents constitute treasuries. The Supreme Principles for Ordering the World (Huangji jingshi), however, discusses them by correlating the four seasons with four Classics. It says: “The four treasuries of august Heaven refer to spring, summer, autumn, and winter; yin and yang rise and fall within them. The four treasuries of the sages refer to the Changes, Documents, Odes, and Spring and Autumn Annals; rites and music flourish and decline within them.” The seasons of Heaven and the Classics of the sages depend upon one another for their fulfillment; all things and all people lie within the four…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
府誠有如邵子之論也學者能究心於此
則經之體天德而前民用者不益會其精
耶欲考史者不必求之浩繁也惟在去五
難而執三長焉何爲五難袁崧曰煩而不
整一難也俗而不典二難也書不實錄三
難也賞罰不中四難也文不勝質五難也
於是去之則能正史之失矣何謂三長劉
知幾謂才以充之而使其不窮學以博之
而使其不偏識以辨之而使其不誣者是
===
也於是執之則能究史之全矣若夫荀悅
有五志之說蓋言達道義彰法戒通古今
著功勳表賢能也而干寶釋之以爲若體
國經野也用兵征伐忠孝貞烈也文告轉
對才力技藝也則從而書之劉知幾有三
科之說蓋言敘沿革明罪惡旌怪異也而
又自釋以爲若禮樂用舍也人物邪正古
今治忽也幽明感應禍福萌兆也則從而
書之蓋志事之書貴有體要信直之史宜
punctuated:
府，誠有如邵子之論也。學者能究心於此，則經之體天德而前民用者，不益會其精耶？

欲考史者，不必求之浩繁也，惟在去五難而執三長焉。何爲五難？袁崧曰：「煩而不整，一難也；俗而不典，二難也；書不實錄，三難也；賞罰不中，四難也；文不勝質，五難也。」於是去之，則能正史之失矣。何謂三長？劉知幾謂才以充之而使其不窮，學以博之而使其不偏，識以辨之而使其不誣者是也。於是執之，則能究史之全矣。

若夫荀悅有五志之說，蓋言達道義、彰法戒、通古今、著功勳、表賢能也。而干寶釋之，以爲若體國經野也，用兵征伐、忠孝貞烈也，文告轉對、才力技藝也，則從而書之。劉知幾有三科之說，蓋言敘沿革、明罪惡、旌怪異也。而又自釋，以爲若禮樂用舍也，人物邪正、古今治忽也，幽明感應、禍福萌兆也，則從而書之。蓋志事之書，貴有體要；信直之史，宜
translation_en:
…repositories: it is indeed as Master Shao argued. If scholars can devote themselves to investigating this, will they not grasp still more fully the essential meaning of how the classics embody Heaven’s virtue and guide the people’s practical activities?

Those wishing to examine history need not seek it amid a vast profusion of writings. What matters is simply to eliminate the five difficulties and uphold the three strengths. What are the five difficulties? Yuan Song said: “Prolixity without order is the first difficulty; vulgarity without refinement is the second; writing that does not faithfully record events is the third; inappropriate rewards and punishments are the fourth; literary expression that does not measure up to its substance is the fifth.” By eliminating these, one can correct the failings of historical writing. What are the three strengths? They are what Liu Zhiji described: talent to give it substance and keep it inexhaustible; learning to give it breadth and keep it free of partiality; and judgment to make distinctions and keep it free of falsehood. By upholding these, one can fully comprehend history in its entirety.

As for Xun Yue’s doctrine of the five aims, these are to convey the Way and righteousness, make exemplary standards and warnings manifest, connect past and present, record meritorious achievements, and give recognition to the worthy and capable. Gan Bao explained these as matters such as organizing the capital and laying out the countryside; deploying troops and conducting punitive campaigns; loyalty, filial devotion, steadfastness, and heroic sacrifice; official proclamations and responses presented in rotation at court; and abilities, skills, and arts—all of which should accordingly be recorded. Liu Zhiji’s doctrine of the three categories refers to recounting continuities and changes, exposing crimes and wrongdoing, and drawing attention to strange and anomalous occurrences. He himself further explained these as matters such as the adoption or abandonment of rites and music; the wickedness or uprightness of individuals; order and disorder in past and present; responses between the unseen and visible realms; and the first portents of calamity and good fortune—all of which should accordingly be recorded. For writings that record events, what is valued is an organizing framework and attention to essentials; truthful and forthright histories ought to …

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
別科條誠有如二家之言也學者能究心
于此則史之備監戒而昭勸懲者不益盡
其變耶雖然有本焉心者道之統會而文
之管攝也故易者言乎心之時也書者言
乎心之中也詩者言乎心之性情也禮樂
者言乎心之和敬也春秋者言乎心之好
惡也論孟者言乎心之道德也故以吾心
求六經論孟以六經論孟而觀經史則其
合此者謂之正離此者謂之叛法此而褒
===
===
貶者謂之公非此而褒貶者謂之私而經
史之得失瞭然無以遁其情矣此博物洽
聞者不免於玩物喪志之譏而據經以立
極觀聖以考言事變錯陳而中持衡焉夫
是以隨在皆實學也久之得意忘言得言
忘象而註脚六經筌蹄諸史亦可矣不然
斃其力於紙上之求而曰此十三經也此
二十一史也入乎耳出乎口楊雄氏所謂
說鈴也而奚益哉愚也非通經博史者也
punctuated: 別科條，誠有如二家之言也。學者能究心于此，則史之備監戒而昭勸懲者，不益盡其變耶？雖然，有本焉。心者，道之統會而文之管攝也。故《易》者，言乎心之時也；《書》者，言乎心之中也；《詩》者，言乎心之性情也；禮樂者，言乎心之和敬也；《春秋》者，言乎心之好惡也；《論》《孟》者，言乎心之道德也。故以吾心求六經、《論》《孟》，以六經、《論》《孟》而觀經史，則其合此者謂之正，離此者謂之叛；法此而褒貶者謂之公，非此而褒貶者謂之私。而經史之得失，瞭然無以遁其情矣。此博物洽聞者不免於玩物喪志之譏，而據經以立極，觀聖以考言，事變錯陳而中持衡焉，夫是以隨在皆實學也。久之，得意忘言，得言忘象，而註脚六經、筌蹄諸史，亦可矣。不然，斃其力於紙上之求，而曰此十三經也，此二十一史也，入乎耳，出乎口，楊雄氏所謂說鈴也，而奚益哉？愚也，非通經博史者也，
translation_en: …distinguish their categories and divisions: it is indeed as these two writers have said. If scholars can devote their minds to this, will they not comprehend still more fully the varied ways in which histories furnish admonitions and make clear what deserves encouragement or punishment? Yet there is a foundation for this. The mind is where the Way converges and what governs writing. Thus, the Book of Changes speaks of the mind’s responsiveness to the times; the Book of Documents, of its equilibrium; the Book of Odes, of its nature and feelings; rites and music, of its harmony and reverence; the Spring and Autumn Annals, of its likes and dislikes; and the Analects and Mencius, of its Way and virtue. Therefore, if we use our own minds to seek understanding of the Six Classics, the Analects, and Mencius, and use these works to examine the classics and histories, whatever accords with this standard is called correct, and whatever departs from it is called deviant. Praise and blame that follow this standard are called impartial; praise and blame that contravene it are called partial. The merits and faults of the classics and histories will then be plain, with their true character nowhere concealed. This is why those with extensive knowledge and wide learning cannot escape the criticism that they lose their purpose through absorption in things. But if one relies on the classics to establish the ultimate standard and looks to the sages to assess statements, then, amid the tangled array of events and changes, one holds the balance within. Thus, wherever one turns, there is substantive learning. In time, having grasped the meaning, one may forget the words; having grasped the words, one may forget the images. It will then be possible to treat the Six Classics as explanatory notes and the histories as fish traps and rabbit snares—means that can be set aside once their purpose is achieved. Otherwise, one exhausts one’s strength in searching upon paper, saying, ‘These are the Thirteen Classics; these are the Twenty-One Histories.’ What enters the ears merely issues from the mouth: this is what Yang Xiong called ‘the tinkling of talk.’ What benefit is there in it? I, in my ignorance, am no one deeply versed in the classics or widely learned in history…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
不忍爲悖經穢史之陋亦不敢蹈擬經譏
史之失惟執事指其迷而歸之道焉固所
願也
第四問
邵晙
同考試官教諭廖批民生休戚係守令之賢
否子於兩漢吏治知所决擇賢矣哉
同考試官教諭鄭批循吏之名盛實之衰也
此作能究王霸名實之辨可觀他日之循良矣
===
考試官學正馮批讀子之文是不以漢吏
自居志趣遠邁良可嘉尚
考試官學正劉批論治識體僅見此篇
知王霸之辨者可以達牧民之政矣知得
失之理者可以定考人之極矣夫民之仰
於治民者如子之仰於父母也父母之於
子所以使之飽煖安逸者不自以爲私而
子之飽煖安逸於父母也亦不以爲德何
者其情本相維也故治民者不以父母之
punctuated:
不忍爲悖經穢史之陋，亦不敢蹈擬經譏史之失，惟執事指其迷而歸之道焉，固所願也。

第四問
邵晙

同考試官教諭廖批：民生休戚係守令之賢否，子於兩漢吏治知所决擇，賢矣哉！

同考試官教諭鄭批：循吏之名盛，實之衰也。此作能究王霸名實之辨，可觀他日之循良矣。

考試官學正馮批：讀子之文，是不以漢吏自居，志趣遠邁，良可嘉尚。

考試官學正劉批：論治識體，僅見此篇。

知王霸之辨者，可以達牧民之政矣；知得失之理者，可以定考人之極矣。夫民之仰於治民者，如子之仰於父母也。父母之於子，所以使之飽煖安逸者，不自以爲私；而子之飽煖安逸於父母也，亦不以爲德。何者？其情本相維也。故治民者不以父母之
translation_en:
…I cannot bear to commit the vulgarity of contradicting the Classics and sullying the histories, nor dare I fall into the error of composing imitations of the Classics and disparaging the histories. That you, sir, should point out my errors and guide me back to the Way is indeed my wish.

Fourth Policy Question
Shao Jun 邵晙

Comment by Associate Examiner Liao, Instructor: The people's well-being and suffering depend upon the worthiness or unworthiness of prefects and magistrates. In considering official administration under the two Han dynasties, you know what to accept and what to reject. How worthy!

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: The flourishing reputation of “exemplary officials” marks the decline of the reality. This essay thoroughly examines the distinctions between kingly and hegemonic rule, and between reputation and reality. It gives a glimpse of the exemplary and benevolent official you will become.

Comment by Examiner Feng, School Instructor: Reading your essay, I see that you do not content yourself with the standard of Han officials. Your aspirations reach far beyond them and truly deserve praise and esteem.

Comment by Examiner Liu, School Instructor: Only in this essay have I seen a discussion of governance that grasps its essentials.

Those who understand the distinction between kingly and hegemonic rule can comprehend the policies for governing the people; those who understand the principles of success and failure can establish the ultimate standard for evaluating officials. The people look up to those who govern them just as children look up to their parents. When parents ensure that their children are well fed, warm, secure, and at ease, they do not regard this as partiality; and when children enjoy food, warmth, security, and ease through their parents, they likewise do not regard this as a special favor. Why is this? Their affections inherently bind them to one another. Thus, when those who govern the people do not employ a parent's…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
心牧之使己之循於人是不以王道治之
也考人者不核之以父母之心使人之循
於己是不以王道勵之也人循於己者己
得而風之則下無惰德而考人之極立矣
己循於人者人得而庇之則上有實惠而
不愧於父母斯民矣王道不易易乎哉嗚
呼審乎此可以言吏治矣執事有感於吏
治之不見於天下也舉兩漢循吏下問夫
固風之以王道也則定去取之極使人知
===
所嚮往以復古循吏之治者豈外於此乎
夫
國家張官置吏以爲民也而守令於民爲最
近所以承君之令而致之民也苟牧民者
以父母斯民爲王道詎深文刻核以羅元
元之不逮如後世乎哉蓋聞至道之世渾
渾爾噩噩爾其政悶悶其民醇醇上下相
忘通貫萬化不言而信不辨而理如天地
無所勞於物而物各得其性物雖各得其
punctuated:
心牧之，使己之循於人，是不以王道治之也。考人者不核之以父母之心，使人之循於己，是不以王道勵之也。人循於己者，己得而風之，則下無惰德，而考人之極立矣；己循於人者，人得而庇之，則上有實惠，而不愧於父母斯民矣。王道不易易乎哉！嗚呼！審乎此，可以言吏治矣。執事有感於吏治之不見於天下也，舉兩漢循吏下問，夫固風之以王道也。則定去取之極，使人知所嚮往，以復古循吏之治者，豈外於此乎？
夫國家張官置吏以爲民也，而守令於民爲最近，所以承君之令而致之民也。苟牧民者以父母斯民爲王道，詎深文刻核，以羅元元之不逮，如後世乎哉？蓋聞至道之世，渾渾爾，噩噩爾，其政悶悶，其民醇醇，上下相忘，通貫萬化，不言而信，不辨而理，如天地無所勞於物，而物各得其性。物雖各得其
translation_en:
…heart to shepherd them, bringing oneself into accord with others: failing to do this is to govern them without the kingly Way. Those who assess others, if they do not examine them with the heart of a parent and bring others into accord with themselves, fail to encourage them through the kingly Way. When others follow oneself, one can influence them; then those below will not neglect virtue, and the standard for assessing others will be established. When one brings oneself into accord with others, they can receive one's protection; then those above bestow tangible benefits and need not be ashamed to act as parents to these people. Is the kingly Way not readily practiced [?]? Alas! Only after examining this thoroughly can one discuss the administration of officials. You, honored examiners, lament that proper official administration is nowhere to be seen throughout the realm. By citing the conscientious officials of the Former and Later Han and condescending to question us about them, you are indeed guiding us through the kingly Way. Thus, in establishing the standard for dismissal and retention, enabling people to know what they should aspire to, and restoring the governance of the conscientious officials of antiquity, could one go beyond this?
The state establishes offices and appoints officials for the people's sake. Prefects and magistrates stand closest to the people: they receive the ruler's commands and convey them to the people. If those who shepherd the people regard acting as their parents as the kingly Way, how could they, as in later ages, interpret the laws harshly and scrutinize people mercilessly, ensnaring the common people for shortcomings they cannot overcome? I have heard that in the age of the utmost Way, all was simple and uncontrived; government was unobtrusive, and the people were honest and sincere. Those above and below were oblivious to one another, and all transformations proceeded in harmony. There was trust without words and order without disputation, just as Heaven and Earth expend no labor upon things, yet each thing realizes its own nature. Although each thing realizes its own…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
性而不知其爲天地之功也不知其功而
循吏之名孰爲其立之是可以觀王道矣
三代以降一變而爲春秋戰國再變而爲
秦漢於是法令刑名之說日熾言道德者
溺其職矣司馬遷以爲極之不可以不反
也故史記立例取周季王相之最賢者繫
之循吏傳以表之復取西漢守相之最酷
烈者繫之酷吏傳以別之其言曰法令者
治之具而非制治清濁之源也吁微矣班
===
固之續西漢書范曄之集東漢書蓋倣史
記凡例而爲之也今攷循吏之在西漢也
於傳僅得六人焉然文翁顯於孝景之世
王成黃霸龔遂朱邑召信臣迭盛於地節
神雀元始之間固不專在一帝也其取人
之嚴也如是豈有所遺歟不然吳公守河
南治平稱爲第一而傳不之採焉安知天
下無復有吳公者乎循吏之在東漢也於
傳僅得十二人焉然衛颯任延王渙許荊
punctuated:
性，而不知其爲天地之功也。不知其功，而循吏之名孰爲其立之？是可以觀王道矣。
三代以降，一變而爲春秋戰國，再變而爲秦漢。於是法令刑名之說日熾，言道德者溺其職矣。司馬遷以爲極之不可以不反也，故史記立例，取周季王相之最賢者，繫之循吏傳以表之；復取西漢守相之最酷烈者，繫之酷吏傳以別之。其言曰：「法令者，治之具，而非制治清濁之源也。」吁，微矣！班固之續西漢書，范曄之集東漢書，蓋倣史記凡例而爲之也。
今攷循吏之在西漢也，於傳僅得六人焉。然文翁顯於孝景之世，王成、黃霸、龔遂、朱邑、召信臣迭盛於地節、神雀、元始之間，固不專在一帝也。其取人之嚴也如是，豈有所遺歟？不然，吳公守河南，治平稱爲第一，而傳不之採焉，安知天下無復有吳公者乎？循吏之在東漢也，於傳僅得十二人焉。然衛颯、任延、王渙、許荊
translation_en:
…their nature, yet do not know that this is the achievement of Heaven and Earth. If that achievement goes unrecognized, who would establish for such officials a reputation as upright officials? Here one may discern the Kingly Way.
After the Three Dynasties, one transformation brought the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, and another brought the Qin and Han. The doctrines of laws, ordinances, punishments, and administrative accountability then grew ever more prevalent, while those who spoke of the Way and virtue were deemed remiss in their duties. Sima Qian believed that, once this had reached its extreme, a reversal was unavoidable. Accordingly, in establishing the arrangement of the Records of the Grand Historian, he selected the worthiest royal ministers of the late Zhou and placed them in the “Biographies of Upright Officials” to commend them. He also selected the most cruel and ruthless commandery administrators and kingdom chancellors of the Western Han and placed them in the “Biographies of Harsh Officials” to distinguish them. He said: “Laws and ordinances are instruments of government, not the source that determines whether government is pure or corrupt.” Ah, how subtle! Ban Gu’s continuation of the historical record in the History of the Western Han and Fan Ye’s compilation of the History of the Eastern Han generally followed the organizational principles of the Records of the Grand Historian.
Now, examining the upright officials of the Western Han, we find only six men in their collected biographies. Yet Wen Weng rose to prominence under Emperor Xiaojing, while Wang Cheng, Huang Ba, Gong Sui, Zhu Yi, and Shao Xinchen successively flourished during the Dijie, Shenjue, and Yuanshi eras. They certainly did not all belong to the reign of a single emperor. With selection so strict, might some have been omitted? Otherwise, Master Wu, while serving as administrator of Henan, was acclaimed as foremost for his peaceful and orderly government, yet the biographies did not include him. How can we know that there were no others like Master Wu throughout the realm? As for the upright officials of the Eastern Han, we find only twelve men in their collected biographies. Yet Wei Sa, Ren Yan, Wang Huan, and Xu Jing…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
顯於光武和帝之世王景秦彭孟嘗第五
訪劉矩仇覽諸人迭見於章肅桓順之朝
亦不止一時也其取人之嚴也如是無亦
有所遺歟不然杜詩守南陽民以杜母見
懷而傳亦未之採焉安知天下無復有杜
詩者乎自今觀之文翁之興學校龔遂之
息盜賊黃霸之課耕桑召信臣之開水利
王成之增戶口朱邑之崇廉平傳之循吏
固矣若郅都之公廉不發私書行法不避
===
貴戚當時畏威名者以蒼鷹號之此其志
亦壯矣雖以廉能別傳可也而固乃列之
酷吏然則以束溼之甯成而賈至千萬以
展月之溫舒而家累千金其人品相去何
如也而乃與都例論乎衛颯之脩禮教秦
彭之明庠序任延之飱孝子劉矩之務信
讓王景之起芍陂王渙之辨寃訟第五訪
之賑饑荒劉寵之除煩苛許荊之感蔣均
仇覽之化陳元孟嘗之革前弊童恢之布
punctuated: 顯於光武、和帝之世，王景、秦彭、孟嘗、第五訪、劉矩、仇覽諸人迭見於章、肅、桓、順之朝，亦不止一時也。其取人之嚴也如是，無亦有所遺歟？不然，杜詩守南陽，民以杜母見懷，而傳亦未之採焉，安知天下無復有杜詩者乎？自今觀之，文翁之興學校，龔遂之息盜賊，黃霸之課耕桑，召信臣之開水利，王成之增戶口，朱邑之崇廉平，傳之循吏固矣。若郅都之公廉，不發私書，行法不避貴戚，當時畏威名者以蒼鷹號之，此其志亦壯矣！雖以廉能別傳可也，而固乃列之酷吏。然則以束溼之甯成而賈至千萬，以展月之溫舒而家累千金，其人品相去何如也，而乃與都例論乎？衛颯之脩禮教，秦彭之明庠序，任延之飱孝子，劉矩之務信讓，王景之起芍陂，王渙之辨寃訟，第五訪之賑饑荒，劉寵之除煩苛，許荊之感蔣均，仇覽之化陳元，孟嘗之革前弊，童恢之布
translation_en:
…were prominent during the reigns of Emperors Guangwu and He. Wang Jing, Qin Peng, Meng Chang, Diwu Fang, Liu Ju, Qiu Lan, and others appeared successively during the reigns of Zhang, Su [?], Huan, and Shun; they too were not confined to a single period. Such was the strictness with which men were selected for inclusion. Might some nevertheless have been omitted? Otherwise, when Du Shi governed Nanyang, the people cherished him as “Mother Du,” yet the biographies did not include him either. How can we know that there were no other men like Du Shi throughout the empire?

Viewed from the present, Wen Weng established schools; Gong Sui suppressed banditry; Huang Ba encouraged farming and sericulture; Shao Xinchen developed irrigation; Wang Cheng increased the registered population; and Zhu Yi upheld integrity and impartiality. Their inclusion in the biographies of exemplary officials was certainly justified. As for Zhi Du, he was impartial and incorruptible: he would not open private letters, and in enforcing the law he spared neither nobles nor imperial relatives. Those of his day who feared his formidable reputation called him the “Goshawk.” His resolve was indeed mighty! It would have been fitting even to give him a separate biography as an upright and capable official, yet Ban Gu placed him among the harsh officials. Now Ning Cheng, whose severity was likened to binding wet bundles, amassed tens of millions through commerce, while Wen Shu, described as “zhan yue” [?], accumulated a family fortune of a thousand jin of gold. How far apart were they from Zhi Du in personal character! Yet could they be discussed in the same category as he?

Wei Sa cultivated ritual instruction; Qin Peng promoted the schools; Ren Yan provided meals for filial sons; Liu Ju devoted himself to trustworthiness and deference; Wang Jing restored the Quebei reservoir; Wang Huan adjudicated cases of injustice; Diwu Fang relieved famine; Liu Chong abolished vexatious and oppressive measures; Xu Jing moved Jiang Jun to reform; Qiu Lan transformed Chen Yuan; Meng Chang eliminated earlier abuses; and Tong Hui spread…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
德政傳之循吏固矣若董宣之平生砥礪
名節蓋棺布被覆體當時畏威名者以臥
虎號之此其氣亦豪矣雖以廉能别傳可
也而曄亦列之酷吏然則黃昌殺登樓之
婦王吉繩夏月之屍其用情公私何如也
而乃與宣例論乎嗟夫史氏之意微矣何
者豈弟君子民之父母而鷹鸇之搏擊不
如烏鳥之慈兩漢吏弊方且以酷爲能其
糜爛不可勝紀彼其禁臨江王之刀筆而
===
致之死窮公孫丹之親黨而繫之獄則都
與宣之爲也而其事亦涉於酷史氏意謂
可使二子受不韙之名而不可使天下受
酷吏之禍故斷斷然列之傳首而不疑此
其立法雖嚴用意甚厚而於王霸之辨有
得其槩者亦挽回風俗之一大機也然就
其中而核之王成增戶口之政固爲僞飾
而黃霸遣吏廉事乃借烏攫之事以伺之
不涉於察乎童恢逢寃虎之訴似爲迂誕
punctuated:
德政，傳之循吏固矣。若董宣之平生砥礪名節，蓋棺布被覆體，當時畏威名者以臥虎號之，此其氣亦豪矣。雖以廉能别傳可也，而曄亦列之酷吏。然則黃昌殺登樓之婦，王吉繩夏月之屍，其用情公私何如也，而乃與宣例論乎？嗟夫！史氏之意微矣。何者？豈弟君子，民之父母，而鷹鸇之搏擊不如烏鳥之慈。兩漢吏弊，方且以酷爲能，其糜爛不可勝紀。彼其禁臨江王之刀筆而致之死，窮公孫丹之親黨而繫之獄，則都與宣之爲也，而其事亦涉於酷。史氏意謂，可使二子受不韙之名，而不可使天下受酷吏之禍，故斷斷然列之傳首而不疑。此其立法雖嚴，用意甚厚，而於王霸之辨有得其槩者，亦挽回風俗之一大機也。
然就其中而核之，王成增戶口之政固爲僞飾，而黃霸遣吏廉事，乃借烏攫之事以伺之，不涉於察乎？童恢逢寃虎之訴，似爲迂誕。
translation_en:
…benevolent government: their inclusion in the biographies of Exemplary Officials is certainly justified. As for Dong Xuan, throughout his life he cultivated his integrity and reputation; when his coffin was closed, a cloth quilt covered his body. Those of his time who feared his formidable reputation called him the “Crouching Tiger.” His spirit, too, was heroic. He might well have received a separate biography for his incorruptibility and ability, yet Fan Ye likewise placed him among the Harsh Officials. Huang Chang killed a woman for ascending a tower, while Wang Ji punished a corpse in the summer months [?]. How did their motives compare in public-mindedness or private interest? Yet they were discussed in the same category as Dong Xuan!
Alas, the historian’s intention was subtle! Why? “The gracious and kindly gentleman is the father and mother of the people”; the striking and seizing of hawks and falcons cannot compare with the tenderness of crows. Among the abuses of officialdom during the two Han dynasties, harshness was being taken for competence, and the devastation it caused was beyond reckoning. Denying the Prince of Linjiang writing implements and thereby bringing about his death, and pursuing Gongsun Dan’s relatives and associates to the utmost and committing them to prison—these were the deeds of Zhi Du and Dong Xuan, and they too partook of harshness. The historian’s intention was that these two men might be made to bear the stigma of wrongdoing, but All-under-Heaven must not be made to suffer the calamities inflicted by harsh officials. Thus he resolutely placed them at the head of those biographies without hesitation. Though strict in establishing this standard, his intention was deeply benevolent. He grasped something of the essential distinction between kingly and hegemonic rule; this, too, was a major means of restoring social customs.
Yet, on examining the accounts themselves, Wang Cheng’s achievement in increasing the registered population was certainly a fabrication. And when Huang Ba sent an officer to investigate affairs, he used an incident involving a crow snatching something away to keep watch over him. Did this not verge on intrusive scrutiny? Tong Hui’s encounter with a plea concerning a wrongly accused tiger seems far-fetched and fanciful…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
而孟嘗反政合浦必舉還珠之事以實之
不幾於怪乎其他形於甘棠之留固出於
兒童里社之所俎豆而希心者也然竊仁
義之似雖足以宜民於一時使以仁義之
實施之則爝火之光自息矣此漢治不免
於雜霸視古之父母斯民者可同日語哉
故牧民者以父母之心行之則渾渾悶悶
之政於是乎在矣彼風行霜烈不足以洽
化懲違視循吏何啻徑庭也方今
===
聖天子勵精圖治禮樂化洽而雍熙大和之治
遠邁兩漢又況考課之法
祖宗成憲俱在監司以時而公其激揚銓部以
時而明其黜陟固宜循吏之風遠追唐虞
之隆矣而博觀郡縣求以當
上意者蓋僅僅見豈司考課者未定取舍之極
使人不知所適從歟愚以爲循之爲義上
順天理下順人情之謂也類非浮薄苛刻
者之所能以今日觀之循良者難求而深
punctuated:
而孟嘗反政合浦，必舉還珠之事以實之，不幾於怪乎？其他形於甘棠之留，固出於兒童里社之所俎豆而希心者也。然竊仁義之似，雖足以宜民於一時，使以仁義之實施之，則爝火之光自息矣。此漢治不免於雜霸，視古之父母斯民者，可同日語哉？故牧民者以父母之心行之，則渾渾悶悶之政於是乎在矣。彼風行霜烈，不足以洽化懲違，視循吏何啻徑庭也！
方今聖天子勵精圖治，禮樂化洽，而雍熙大和之治遠邁兩漢。又況考課之法，祖宗成憲俱在，監司以時而公其激揚，銓部以時而明其黜陟，固宜循吏之風遠追唐虞之隆矣。而博觀郡縣，求以當上意者，蓋僅僅見。豈司考課者未定取舍之極，使人不知所適從歟？愚以爲循之爲義，上順天理，下順人情之謂也，類非浮薄苛刻者之所能。以今日觀之，循良者難求，而深
translation_en:
…Yet when Meng Chang reformed the administration of Hepu [?], the account insists on citing the return of the pearls to substantiate his achievement: does this not verge on the fabulous? Other achievements, expressed in the preservation of the sweet pear tree, certainly arose from deeds that children and village communities honored with offerings and aspired to emulate. Yet appropriating the semblance of benevolence and righteousness, though sufficient to benefit the people for a time, is like the light of a small torch: once genuine benevolence and righteousness are put into practice, that light dies out of itself. Han government thus remained mixed with the methods of hegemonic rule. Can it be spoken of in the same breath as the government of those ancients who acted as fathers and mothers to the people? When those who shepherd the people act with a parent's heart, their government will possess that uncontrived simplicity and unobtrusiveness. Those whose measures sweep like the wind and bite like frost cannot extend moral transformation throughout the realm or restrain transgression. How vast is the distance between them and the exemplary officials!
Today our sagely Son of Heaven devotes his energies to good government. The transforming influence of rites and music is pervasive, and his reign of concord, prosperity, and supreme harmony far surpasses the two Han dynasties. Moreover, the established statutes of the imperial ancestors governing the evaluation of officials remain fully in force. The surveillance officials periodically and impartially censure and commend, while the Ministry of Personnel periodically makes clear its decisions on demotion and promotion. Surely, then, the exemplary officials' tradition ought to rival the flourishing age of Tang and Yu. Yet a broad survey of prefectures and counties reveals scarcely any officials who meet His Majesty's intentions. Could those responsible for evaluating officials have failed to establish a definitive standard for acceptance and rejection, leaving men uncertain what course to follow? In my humble view, the meaning of xun, the quality of an exemplary official, is to accord above with the principles of Heaven and below with human feelings. This is generally beyond the ability of the frivolous and harsh. Judging by conditions today, exemplary and benevolent officials are difficult to find, while those who are harsh …

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
文者難辨也今夫廉幹華藻之吏人人而
知之矣反是而簡靜而悃愊日計不足月
計有餘固勤於民事者也苟非詳察而優
養之其不以不職考者鮮矣當是時縱有
陽城之心勞倪寬之課殿夫安得而用之
今夫貪墨酷暴之吏人人而知之矣外是
而飾行而文姦迎合鍛鍊巧詆誣服固厚
於虐民者也苟非徐觀而捄正之其不以
稱職考者鮮矣當是時即有訊鼠之張湯
===
蝮鷙之殷周又安得而黜之然則明好惡
之分示趨向之的容外求乎孔子曰君子
之德風也小人之德草也何者感應之機
在我也苟考人者以深文爲忌以循良爲
尚而有聲於郡縣者請
璽書褒美增秩加官不少靳焉使天下之爲守
令者曉然知
上所以惇元元之意而以過刻爲戒是使人之
循於我也而天下之人亦以父母斯民爲
punctuated: 文者難辨也。今夫廉幹華藻之吏，人人而知之矣。反是而簡靜而悃愊，日計不足，月計有餘，固勤於民事者也。苟非詳察而優養之，其不以不職考者鮮矣。當是時，縱有陽城之心勞、倪寬之課殿，夫安得而用之？今夫貪墨酷暴之吏，人人而知之矣。外是而飾行而文姦，迎合鍛鍊，巧詆誣服，固厚於虐民者也。苟非徐觀而捄正之，其不以稱職考者鮮矣。當是時，即有訊鼠之張湯、蝮鷙之殷周，又安得而黜之？然則明好惡之分，示趨向之的，容外求乎？孔子曰：「君子之德風也，小人之德草也。」何者？感應之機在我也。苟考人者以深文爲忌，以循良爲尚，而有聲於郡縣者，請璽書褒美，增秩加官，不少靳焉，使天下之爲守令者曉然知上所以惇元元之意，而以過刻爲戒，是使人之循於我也。而天下之人亦以父母斯民爲
translation_en:
…those who manipulate the letter of the law are difficult to distinguish. Officials known for integrity, administrative ability, and literary brilliance are recognized by everyone. By contrast, those who are unassuming, quiet, and sincere may seem to accomplish too little when assessed by the day, yet more than enough when assessed by the month: they are indeed diligent in attending to the people’s affairs. Unless they are examined carefully and generously supported, few will escape being rated incompetent. Under such circumstances, even a man with Yang Cheng’s devoted labors, or one ranked last in his assessment like Ni Kuan, could hardly be employed. Officials who are corrupt, cruel, and violent are recognized by everyone. Beyond these, however, there are those who embellish their conduct and disguise their wickedness, curry favor and fabricate charges, make cunning accusations and force false confessions: these are indeed deeply engaged in oppressing the people. Unless they are observed patiently and their conduct corrected, few will fail to be rated competent. Under such circumstances, even a Zhang Tang who interrogated a rat, or men as venomous as vipers and fierce as birds of prey, like Yin and Zhou [?], could hardly be dismissed.

Then, to make clear the distinction between what is approved and what is condemned, and to indicate the proper direction to follow, can one look elsewhere? Confucius said: “The virtue of the gentleman is wind; the virtue of the petty man is grass.” Why is this so? The impulse that elicits a response lies with us. If those who assess others shun harsh manipulation of the law and esteem conscientious, benevolent administration, then, for officials who have earned a good reputation in the prefectures and counties, they should request imperial letters of commendation under seal, increases in rank, and promotions in office, without the least stinting. This would enable prefects and magistrates throughout the realm to understand clearly His Majesty’s intention to care generously for the common people, and to guard against excessive severity. In this way we would lead others to follow our example. And men throughout the realm would likewise make acting as fathers and mothers to these people their …

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
心惟知養和氣以待造化之自定則化續
羔羊而陋兩漢於不足者非所以風之哉
然此
國家已試之效也顧操柄者力行何如耳執
事以爲何如
第五問
陳錫
同考試官教諭吳批觀拯荒一策切中機宜
經國遠猷端有望于子矣
===
考試官學正馮批此策裕國計濟時艱籌
畫俱善是有志于用世者
考試官學正劉批湖以西水災爲劇子以
蠲租恤民爲對剴切著明經濟之學於此試之
通天下之變者達其權而已矣識天下之
幾者定其經而已矣夫事幾之乘也其變
每生於無常而圖理之道其法必期於可
久故相時以計其變則權宜審而無妄動
之弊先時以察其幾則經畫周而無臨事
punctuated:
心，惟知養和氣以待造化之自定，則化續羔羊而陋兩漢於不足者，非所以風之哉？然此國家已試之效也，顧操柄者力行何如耳。執事以爲何如？
第五問
陳錫
同考試官教諭吳批：觀拯荒一策，切中機宜，經國遠猷，端有望于子矣。
考試官學正馮批：此策裕國計、濟時艱，籌畫俱善，是有志于用世者。
考試官學正劉批：湖以西水災爲劇，子以蠲租恤民爲對，剴切著明，經濟之學於此試之。
通天下之變者，達其權而已矣；識天下之幾者，定其經而已矣。夫事幾之乘也，其變每生於無常，而圖理之道，其法必期於可久。故相時以計其變，則權宜審而無妄動之弊；先時以察其幾，則經畫周而無臨事
translation_en:
…as their guiding concern, knowing only to nurture harmonious vital forces and await the natural settling of the processes of creation. Would this not inspire a moral transformation continuing that celebrated in “The Lamb” and making even the two Han dynasties seem inferior? These, moreover, are results already demonstrated by our dynasty; it depends only on how vigorously those who wield authority put these measures into practice. What do you, honored examiners, think?
Fifth Policy Question
Chen Xi
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Instructor: Your proposal for relieving famine precisely fits the needs of the occasion. We may indeed look to you for far-reaching plans for governing the state.
Comment by Examiner Feng, Instructor: This policy essay offers sound planning both for strengthening state finances and for overcoming the difficulties of the times. Its author aspires to serve the world.
Comment by Examiner Liu, Instructor: Flooding has been most severe west of the lake. You respond by proposing remission of land taxes and relief for the people; your arguments are pertinent, clear, and explicit. Here your learning in statecraft is put to the test.
To comprehend the changes of the world requires only mastery of expedient adaptation; to discern the first signs of events in the world requires only the establishment of constant principles. When incipient developments arise, their changes often emerge unpredictably, yet the methods used in planning good governance must aim at lasting effectiveness. Thus, by assessing present circumstances and reckoning with their changes, one judges expedient measures carefully and avoids the harm of rash action; by discerning incipient developments ahead of time, one makes comprehensive plans and avoids, when affairs arise…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
之失此善於裕民者必窮源探本而不爲
一朝一夕之計者其所慮者遠也不然患
生而爲之謀事至而爲之備吁亦晩矣執
事念兩浙之水災而追論乎往事誠有見
於古今之效而欲以捄之者也爲下爲民
之心切矣承學不敏敢不悉心以對夫兩
浙古揚州之地厥田下下厥賦下上上錯
自錢鏐捍海以來富庶甲於天下我
太祖奄有一統邃土宇而版圖之屹然爲東南
===
一財府也
京師軍國百萬之需多倚辦焉然天下形勢
東南爲最下兩浙跨有吳越襟海帶江地
故多水迺者淫雨浹旬江湖竝溢歲登不
給民食滋艱司牧者可晏然已哉崇寛恤
之議者必曰請蠲征矣然
國家經費不容輕損況恃此以捄嗷嗷待哺
之民其可及乎廣賑貸之策者必曰散儲
積矣而郡縣儲蓄未之前聞欲賴升合之
punctuated:
之失。此善於裕民者，必窮源探本，而不爲一朝一夕之計者，其所慮者遠也。不然，患生而爲之謀，事至而爲之備，吁，亦晩矣！執事念兩浙之水災，而追論乎往事，誠有見於古今之效，而欲以捄之者也。爲下爲民之心切矣！承學不敏，敢不悉心以對？夫兩浙，古揚州之地，厥田下下，厥賦下上上錯。自錢鏐捍海以來，富庶甲於天下。我太祖奄有一統，邃土宇而版圖之，屹然爲東南一財府也。京師軍國百萬之需，多倚辦焉。
然天下形勢，東南爲最下。兩浙跨有吳越，襟海帶江，地故多水。迺者淫雨浹旬，江湖竝溢，歲登不給，民食滋艱。司牧者可晏然已哉？崇寛恤之議者，必曰請蠲征矣。然國家經費，不容輕損。況恃此以捄嗷嗷待哺之民，其可及乎？廣賑貸之策者，必曰散儲積矣。而郡縣儲蓄，未之前聞，欲賴升合之
translation_en:
…the failure to act properly when events arise. Those skilled at enriching the people invariably investigate the source and probe the roots, making plans that extend beyond a single morning or evening, because their concerns reach far ahead. Otherwise, to devise plans only after trouble arises and make preparations only when events are upon us—alas, that is already too late! Concerned about flooding in the Two Zhe regions, you have looked back and discussed earlier events. You truly discern the results of measures past and present and wish thereby to bring relief. How earnest is your concern for those below and for the people! Though slow-witted in my studies, how could I dare not devote my whole mind to answering?
The Two Zhe regions formed part of ancient Yangzhou: “Its fields were of the lowest of the lower grades; its tribute was of the highest of the lower grades, with higher assessments intermixed.” Since Qian Liu built defenses against the sea, its wealth and population have ranked foremost in the realm. Our Taizu united all under his rule, extended his territorial domain [?], and incorporated this region into the imperial registers and maps. It stood firmly established as a treasury of the southeast. The capital’s military and governmental requirements, amounting to millions, have depended largely upon it.
Yet in the terrain of the realm, the southeast lies lowest. The Two Zhe regions encompass Wu and Yue, with the sea at their breast and the river about their waist; their lands consequently have abundant waters. Recently, incessant rain continued for ten days, and rivers and lakes overflowed together. The year’s harvest is insufficient, and the people’s difficulty in obtaining food grows ever greater. Can those charged with governing them simply remain at ease? Those who advocate leniency and relief will surely say that tax remissions should be requested. Yet the state’s regular revenues cannot lightly be reduced. Moreover, if one relies on this to save people crying out to be fed, can relief reach them in time? Those who propose expanding relief grants and loans will surely say that stored reserves should be distributed. Yet we have heard of no reserves in the prefectures and counties. To hope to rely upon a few sheng or ge of…

title: 嘉靖二十八年浙江鄉試錄
text:
入以濟其衆其可得乎夫旱乾水溢天之
數也所以弭其災而救其患者人之責也
在昔聖人於水旱之來不委之適然之數
而圖惟救濟者恒兢兢焉故雖歷九年之
水七年之旱而國無捐瘠者蓄積多而預
備具法制立而機宜審也詎恃蠲貸之令
以苟幸於一時已哉嘗考漢武帝有逋貸
之蠲矣吳嘉禾有逋賦之寛矣晉惠帝有
戸調絹綿之除矣唐宣宗有免度支鹽鐵
===
之議矣宋高宗有免官司債負和買役錢
之令矣然皆名而已耳是數君者豈誠不
知民生之當念哉備之不豫處之不審則
其勢不得不𠃔耳然其間又有不欲盡免
而權宜於其中者如宋哲宗時令諸路屢
年負欠以十分爲率每年帶納一分似便
民矣及蘇軾訪問濠壽父老又有豐年不
如凶年之說蓋以天災流行苟非太甚民
雖乏食猶可節縮以聊生若豐年舉催積
punctuated:
入以濟其衆，其可得乎？夫旱乾水溢，天之數也；所以弭其災而救其患者，人之責也。在昔聖人於水旱之來，不委之適然之數，而圖惟救濟者恒兢兢焉。故雖歷九年之水、七年之旱，而國無捐瘠者，蓄積多而預備具，法制立而機宜審也。詎恃蠲貸之令，以苟幸於一時已哉？

嘗考漢武帝有逋貸之蠲矣，吳嘉禾有逋賦之寛矣，晉惠帝有戸調絹綿之除矣，唐宣宗有免度支鹽鐵之議矣，宋高宗有免官司債負、和買、役錢之令矣。然皆名而已耳。是數君者，豈誠不知民生之當念哉？備之不豫，處之不審，則其勢不得不𠃔耳。然其間又有不欲盡免而權宜於其中者，如宋哲宗時，令諸路屢年負欠，以十分爲率，每年帶納一分，似便民矣。及蘇軾訪問濠壽父老，又有豐年不如凶年之說。蓋以天災流行，苟非太甚，民雖乏食，猶可節縮以聊生；若豐年舉催積
translation_en:
…receipts to provide relief for so many people—could this be achieved? Droughts and floods belong to the workings of Heaven; mitigating their devastation and rescuing those who suffer from them are human responsibilities. When floods and droughts came, the sages of old did not leave matters to chance and fate, but remained constantly vigilant in planning relief. Thus, although they endured nine years of flooding and seven years of drought, none in the realm were abandoned to starvation: their reserves were ample and their preparations complete, their regulations established and their practical measures carefully considered. How could they merely have relied on orders for remissions and relief loans, hoping for a fortunate outcome for the moment?

I have examined the precedents: Emperor Wu of Han remitted overdue loans; during the Jiahe reign of Wu, relief was granted on tax arrears; Emperor Hui of Jin abolished household levies of silk cloth and silk floss; under Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, there was a proposal to remit levies administered by the revenue and salt-and-iron authorities [?]; and Emperor Gaozong of Song issued orders remitting debts owed to government offices, compulsory government purchases, and service-exemption payments. Yet these were all merely nominal measures. Could these rulers really have failed to recognize that the people’s livelihood deserved their concern? Because they had not prepared in advance or considered their response carefully, circumstances left them no choice but to grant such concessions [?]. Among them, however, some were unwilling to remit everything and instead adopted expedients. Under Emperor Zhezong of Song, for example, orders required the circuits to divide arrears accumulated over successive years into ten parts and collect one part each year alongside current dues. This seemed beneficial to the people. Yet when Su Shi questioned the elders of Haozhou and Shouzhou, they said that a good harvest year was worse than a bad one. For when natural disasters occurred, provided they were not too severe, the people, though short of food, could still economize enough to sustain life. But if, in a good harvest year, collection was pressed for all the accumulated…
